design_detail: Narrative review by a clinical pharmacologist of what can be inferred about drug concentrations and effects during life from samples taken after death: qualitative tests (false positives and false negatives), quantitative analysis, lethal doses and concentrations, tolerance, changes with sampling site and time after death (post-mortem redistribution), the relation between concentrations before and after death, whether a drug's properties predict redistribution, and how a lethal concentration could in principle be defined. The author states that it rests on a systematic search (EMBASE 1974 to June 2007; Medline 1950 to June 2007; text words for post-mortem redistribution), reference lists and a personal collection, but gives no inclusion criteria, counts or appraisal. One table of approximate pharmacokinetic values and heart-to-femoral (central-to-peripheral) post-mortem blood ratios for 32 drugs (ratios from Leikin and Watson 2003), with the author's own correlations; five figures (two scatter plots, three schematic). Read with the editorial in the same issue by J. M. Ritter, the journal's Editor-in-Chief (Br J Clin Pharmacol 2008;66(4):427–429; DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2125.2008.03293.x; PMC2561124), which endorses the review.
can_establish: The mechanisms by which drug concentrations measured after death can differ from those during life, illustrated with the cases, small series and animal experiments published up to mid-2007, and the argument, and the study design it proposes, for defining a lethal concentration.
cannot_establish: How large or how frequent post-mortem changes are for any drug in routine casework (no systematic synthesis or appraisal; the examples are single cases, small series and animal studies), or how well post-mortem concentrations separate deaths caused by a drug from other deaths (no such comparison is made); its own correlations rest on approximate published ratios without uncertainty and cannot be reproduced from its table.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence cited includes single autopsy cases; Rouzioux's 10 cases (1980); Milroy and Forrest's 111 methadone deaths; Jones and Holmgren's 693 deaths from acute alcohol poisoning; a few dozen paired samples taken before and after death; animal experiments in rats, rabbits and swine; and Leikin and Watson's table of heart-to-femoral ratios.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Search stated: EMBASE 1974 to June 2007 for autopsy with drug blood level, Medline 1950 to June 2007 for autopsy with tissue distribution, both also for post-mortem and redistribution as text words, plus reference lists and a personal collection. No inclusion criteria, numbers screened or included, or language limits are given (Search strategy).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the author to illustrate the problems of interpretation, including well-known criminal cases (Shipman, Palmer, Litvinenko) and single cases. Large datasets comparing deaths caused by a drug with other deaths are mentioned in one paragraph (Druid and Holmgren 1997; Reis et al. 2007) without their results.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). The concentrations discussed come from whole blood after death (femoral, heart or other sites), from tissues and fluids, and from plasma or serum during life.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; the review stresses that after death the dose taken cannot be established.
exposure.polysubstance: Raised as a further difficulty: more than one drug is commonly implicated in a death, and interactions between drugs, or between a drug and ethanol, make interpretation harder still (Importance of tolerance, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The review proposes the comparison that would be needed: deaths in which a drug is found assigned to drug-induced or not drug-induced without knowledge of the measured concentrations, then the two concentration distributions compared.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review names tolerance, hypersensitivity (a sub-therapeutic penicillin concentration can kill a person with anaphylaxis), pharmacogenetic variation and hidden causes of sudden death such as arrhythmia as factors that blur any relation between concentration and death.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data collection). The author's own analysis correlates the heart-to-femoral ratio with the volume of distribution (r = 0.247, P > 0.1) and with the octanol–water partition coefficient (r = 0.035, P > 0.1), using approximate ratios from Leikin and Watson (2003) and handbook values (Table 1; Figures 1 and 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The author notes that the published ratios carry no stated uncertainty, which he calls 'undoubtedly very large'.
outcomes.operationalization: Extent of post-mortem redistribution = heart (central) to femoral (peripheral) blood concentration ratio, with a ratio above 3.0 taken as marked redistribution.

analysis.effect_sizes: Second-hand figures as cited (see key findings). The author's correlations: r = 0.247 with volume of distribution and r = 0.035 with the partition coefficient, both P > 0.1. Editors' recalculation from Table 1: r = 0.22 with volume of distribution (31 drugs with a value), 0.09 with the raw and 0.35 with the log partition coefficient (32 drugs; p about 0.05 for the latter); a correlation of 0.247 from about 31 drugs has a 95% interval of about −0.12 to 0.55 (Fisher z), so the data do not exclude a moderate relationship.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable to a narrative review; the choice of examples is the author's.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the correlations rest on about 31 drugs, too few to exclude a moderate correlation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The cited evidence shows, case by case, that post-mortem concentrations can differ from those measured during life: in the few human cases with both, post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios for drugs run from 1.0 (salicylate) to 17.66 (chloroquine), depending on drug, site and time, and two carbon monoxide deaths had concentrations about 25–30% lower after death; that heart blood exceeds femoral blood by about 1.4 to 4 times for 32 drugs (approximate published ratios); that quoted 'lethal' ranges are very wide and overlap (methadone ranges between 60 and 4500 µg/L across sources; MDMA 40–8500 µg/L); that tolerance shifts the relation between concentration and effect (ethanol in 693 poisoning deaths ranged about threefold); and that qualitative results can be falsely positive or falsely negative. It contains no study comparing concentrations in deaths caused by a drug with those in other deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that post-mortem changes make the assumptions of clinical pharmacology largely invalid and interpretation difficult or impossible, and that compilations of lethal concentrations are misleading; the Conclusion that there is "no reliable or obvious connection" between concentrations in life and after death. These are fair readings of most of the examples, though a few show little change after death (salicylate 1.0 and paracetamol 1.5 in single cases; little redistribution of moclobemide, as cited). The examples rest on single cases, small series and animal studies without appraisal, and the review does not weigh the large comparisons of drug deaths against other deaths that it mentions. Its proposed remedy (assigning deaths independently of concentration, then comparing) is stated as a requirement, not tested. Ritter's editorial endorses the review without qualification and says post-mortem measurements are not at present useful in establishing the cause of death, while hoping that measurements in appropriate tissues at defined intervals may become so.

timeline.event: Holt and Benstead find different digoxin concentrations in three post-mortem blood samples from one body (as summarized in the review).

Rouzioux reports 10 cases: in 8, post-mortem left-ventricular concentrations were 2.58 to 17.66 times those during life; in 2 carbon monoxide deaths, 25–30% lower (as summarized). The review's later list of this author's ratios includes an imipramine case at 1.39, below this range (see reporting issues).
Koren and MacLeod name post-mortem redistribution in a rat study of digoxin (as summarized).
Pounder and Jones call post-mortem drug redistribution a toxicological nightmare (cited as reference 7).
Druid and Holmgren compile femoral-blood concentrations of drugs in fatal and control cases from Swedish data (mentioned in the review without results).

Leikin and Watson, 'what the dead can and cannot tell us': source of the heart-to-femoral ratios in Table 1 and of the suggestion that drugs with a volume of distribution above 3 L/kg are candidates for redistribution.
This review, with Ritter's endorsing editorial in the same issue (DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2125.2008.03293.x).

Launiainen and Ojanperä cite the review in their introduction and report post-mortem femoral-blood medians above therapeutic plasma ranges for 46 of 129 drugs in 57,903 Finnish autopsy cases (read in this round).
Borra et al.: review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: A frequently cited statement of the case against reading post-mortem concentrations as if they were concentrations during life, endorsed by the journal's editor. Later database work (for example Launiainen and Ojanperä 2014) supports its central point with large numbers. Its figures are second-hand and should be cited from the primary sources; claims resting only on this review stay at draft and say that their figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

funding.funder: Not reported: the PMC full text has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no competing-interest statement appears in the PMC full text. The author thanks five colleagues for discussions and suggestions.
funding.affiliations_note: West Midlands Centre for Adverse Drug Reactions, City Hospital, and Department of Clinical Pharmacology, University of Birmingham. The author's own book on forensic pharmacology is reference 1; the review relies on others' studies. The accompanying editorial is by the journal's Editor-in-Chief, J. M. Ritter (role stated in the editorial's author information on PMC; Department of Clinical Pharmacology, King's College and St Thomas' Hospitals, London), and carries no funding or conflict statement either. Received 16 February 2008, accepted 19 May 2008.

what_would_settle_it: The study the review itself calls for: a large series of deaths in which a drug was found, each assigned to drug-induced or not drug-induced by assessors blind to the measured concentrations, with standardized femoral sampling at recorded intervals after death, comparing the two concentration distributions (and, for a subset, paired samples from before and after death) to estimate how far they overlap.

domains.note: Databases, years and index terms are stated, which is more than most narrative reviews give, but there are no inclusion criteria, counts or flow, and a personal collection was added; the choice of examples is the author's.

No formal appraisal; the author does name some weaknesses (published ratios without uncertainty, few animals and time points, unpaired samples in the swine study), but the cited case-level figures are taken at face value, and several citations appear mismatched (references 68, 75 and 82).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The evidence is from other investigators; the author cites his own book and one classification paper.

The schematic figures are labelled as schemes and the proposed design is clearly a proposal, but the abstract and Conclusion state the inferences more absolutely than single cases and small series can support, and three of the author's own calculations are misreported (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether post-mortem concentrations can be interpreted
domains.note: The review assembles evidence of uncertainty; large controlled compilations that compare concentrations in drug deaths with those in other deaths (Druid and Holmgren; Reis et al.), the side that could show where femoral concentrations do discriminate, are mentioned without their results.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain. The review is careful and its direction is consistent with later large studies, but its evidence is illustrative rather than systematic and several of its own numbers are misreported. Citable for: the mechanisms by which post-mortem concentrations differ from those during life (redistribution from lungs, heart muscle, gut and bladder; post-mortem generation of ethanol and GHB; hydrolysis of morphine conjugates; changes in protein binding and pH); that heart blood commonly exceeds femoral blood; that qualitative tests can be falsely positive or negative; that quoted lethal ranges overlap widely; that tolerance shifts concentration–effect relations; and the argument that lethal concentrations can only be defined by comparing deaths assigned without knowledge of concentrations. Not citable, except through the primary sources, for any specific ratio or range; and not for the claim that volume of distribution does not predict redistribution, which rests on a correlation that cannot be reproduced from the review's own table.

key_findings.finding: Scope and method: a review of what can be inferred about pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics during life from data obtained after death, based on EMBASE (1974 to June 2007) and Medline (1950 to June 2007) searches with stated index terms, text words for post-mortem redistribution, reference lists and a personal collection.

Qualitative results can mislead in both directions. False positives: immunoassays detecting endogenous digoxin-like substances in renal failure; standard analyses that do not distinguish active R-methadone from almost inactive S-methadone; ethanol and GHB generated after death; contamination from soil, burial containers or lithium-heparin tubes. False negatives: specific tests not done (polonium in the Litvinenko case after negative radiation screens); drug gone before death (paracetamol by the time of death from liver failure; paraquat weeks after ingestion). Opiates can be detected in urine after eating poppy-seed cake. A positive test does not establish that a substance caused death, nor a negative one that it did not.
key_findings.locator: Qualitative post-mortem analysis, 2nd paragraph; False-positive results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; False-negative results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: A Swiss study is cited as finding that the medical history plays an important role in interpreting post-mortem data in about 70% of cases; accounts documented before death are favoured because bias and deception can affect histories taken afterwards.

Quantitative analysis: drug assays commonly have accuracy and precision standard deviations above 10% of the mean; almost all post-mortem analysis is of whole blood whereas reference values in life are mostly from plasma or serum, and the whole-blood-to-plasma ratio varies by drug even in life (0.5 for phenytoin, 2 for maprotiline); femoral venous blood is thought least susceptible to post-mortem change; sedimentation, clotting, haemolysis, putrefaction and contamination can make blood results unhelpful and cavity fluids meaningless.

Approximate heart-to-femoral post-mortem blood ratios for 32 drugs (from Leikin and Watson 2003) range from 1.4 (phenytoin) to 4 (chlorpromazine, midazolam); for example amitriptyline 3.1, oxycodone 3.1, propoxyphene 3.5, haloperidol 3.6, morphine 2.2, codeine 1.8, dextroamphetamine 2, ketamine 1.6, diazepam 1.6. In 11 cases with fentanyl, the ratio ranged from 0.89 to 3.2 (mean 1.6).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Can the extent of post-mortem redistribution be deduced from the properties of a drug?, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand, approximate values without uncertainty, as the author says; cite the primary source for any single ratio.

key_findings.finding: The author reports a weak relation between the heart-to-femoral ratio and the volume of distribution (r = 0.247, P > 0.1) and none with the octanol–water partition coefficient (r = 0.035, P > 0.1), and that the ratio exceeds the volume of distribution in L/kg for 15 of 33 drugs; he notes that other authors have already concluded that volume of distribution cannot be the sole determinant of redistribution (reference 81, a study of three beta-blockers in rabbits), and concludes that it does not indicate an upper limit for the divergence between samples taken before and after death.
key_findings.locator: Can the extent of post-mortem redistribution be deduced from the properties of a drug?, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, footnote; Figures 1 and 2, captions
key_findings.note: Not reproducible from Table 1 (editors' calculation: r = 0.22 with volume of distribution; 0.09 or 0.35 with the raw or log partition coefficient; ratio above volume of distribution for 9 of 31 drugs); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Ratios of post-mortem to ante-mortem concentrations in the few human cases with both: imipramine 4.85, 1.39, 9.94 and 7.60 and chloroquine 17.66 and 14.6 (Rouzioux); post-mortem femoral to ante-mortem serum amitriptyline 3.6, 4.3 and 12, imipramine 3.0 and 6.0; chloroquine ante-mortem serum to post-mortem peripheral 0.7, with heart to peripheral 2.9; MDMA 1.1 to 6.6 and MDA 1.5 to 13.3; single cases of dosulepin 11.7, propoxyphene 8.3, amitriptyline 3.9, methadone 2.6, propranolol 1.9, paracetamol 1.5, salicylate 1.0; diltiazem 1.7.
key_findings.locator: Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Single cases and very small series with varying sample timing, cited second-hand. Rouzioux's imipramine ratio of 1.39 lies below the range of 2.58 to 17.66 that the review gives earlier for 8 of the 10 cases in the same work (Site-related and time-related differences, 1st paragraph); sampling site or timing may differ but is not stated (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Published lethal concentrations overlap widely: quoted ranges of 40–8500 µg/L for MDMA and 60–3100 µg/L for methadone; for methadone in post-mortem blood, Milroy and Forrest found quoted ranges of 220–3040, 200–4500, 320–3980, 1000–2000 and 100–2500 or 100–2600 µg/L, and 84–2700 µg/L in their own 111 cases; in 25 of their cases with arm and leg blood, the author computes a median difference of 72 (printed as µmol/L; interquartile range 20–200).
key_findings.locator: Extrapolation from post-mortem concentrations to ante-mortem concentrations
key_findings.note: The unit of the arm–leg difference is probably misprinted; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Tolerance: for opioids there is little or no separation between therapeutic and toxic concentrations, and receptor downregulation in regular use shifts concentration–response curves; amounts that would kill people without tolerance are tolerated by people who use heroin habitually. Ethanol: a 'lethal' concentration above 500 mg/100 mL has been quoted, yet one patient was still talking above 1500 mg/100 mL; in 693 deaths from acute alcohol poisoning, post-mortem concentrations averaged 356 mg/100 mL, with a spread (printed as a 95% confidence interval) of 185 to 526 mg/100 mL, about threefold between people. More than one drug is commonly implicated in a death.
key_findings.locator: Importance of tolerance, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Making deduction from post-mortem drug concentrations, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mechanisms of post-mortem change: diffusion from the stomach (ethanol), bladder (a single case with femoral diphenhydramine and dihydrocodeine an order of magnitude above heart blood), lungs (lipophilic basic drugs such as amitriptyline, chlorpromazine and methadone, raising left-ventricular and aortic concentrations) and heart muscle (digoxin); in rabbits, MDMA in heart blood rose mainly by redistribution from lung tissue; hydrolysis of conjugates raises apparent free morphine; serum potassium rises from about 3.5 mmol/L before death to 18 at 1 hour and 25 at 24 hours after death. Calculating a body burden from a post-mortem concentration and a volume of distribution measured in life should be abandoned.
key_findings.locator: Site-related and time-related differences in post-mortem concentrations, 4th paragraph; Transfer across barriers, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Redistribution of absorbed drug, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Influence of volume of distribution, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Animal studies: in swine given intravenous morphine, the heart-to-femoral ratio for free morphine was about 0.5 at 30 minutes after death and 1.0 at 120 minutes; in rats dying within 10 minutes of a diamorphine overdose, lung morphine was nearly 10 times heart-blood morphine. Morphine metabolite ratios vary up to 40-fold between living patients, so deductions from post-mortem metabolite ratios are uncertain. A ratio of 1 between heart and femoral blood does not show that the post-mortem concentration equals the concentration before death.
key_findings.locator: Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Proposed standard for defining a lethal concentration: assign a series of deaths in which the drug is found to drug-induced and not drug-induced groups without knowledge of the measured concentrations, then compare the distributions; broad overlap is expected, so there is no clear lethal concentration. Conclusion: concentrations after death cannot generally be read back to concentrations before death, lethal concentrations are extremely difficult to define, post-mortem concentrations have been over-interpreted, and good evidence should be required before lethal concentrations are defined.
key_findings.locator: Making deduction from post-mortem drug concentrations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 5 caption; Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Ritter's editorial (same issue) endorses the review: death makes the assumptions of clinical pharmacology largely invalid, compilations of lethal concentrations are unreliable, clinical pharmacologists without forensic training should hesitate to give expert opinions on post-mortem data, and post-mortem drug measurements are not at present useful in establishing the cause of death, though measurements in appropriate tissues at defined intervals might become so.
key_findings.locator: Beware drawing inferences from drug analyses in post-mortem samples, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The correlations cannot be reproduced from Table 1, whose footnote gives the same coefficients as Figures 1 and 2: from the 31 drugs with a volume of distribution, r = 0.22 (printed 0.247); from the 32 drugs with a partition coefficient, r = 0.09 for the raw value (Table 1 footnote) or 0.35 for its logarithm (Figure 2), printed 0.035 with P > 0.1. The text's ratio above the volume of distribution for 15 of 33 drugs is 9 of 31 in Table 1 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and footnote; Can the extent of post-mortem redistribution be deduced..., 2nd paragraph; Figures 1 and 2, captions
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the figures use a different, unlisted set of 33 drugs or the values are misreported; with the log partition coefficient the Table 1 data give a correlation of 0.35 (p about 0.05), so the statement that drug properties show no relation to redistribution should not be cited from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: For 693 deaths from acute alcohol poisoning, 185 to 526 mg/100 mL is called the 95% confidence interval around the mean of 356; it is the mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations (implied SD 87), a range of individual values. The confidence interval of the mean would be about 350 to 363 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Importance of tolerance, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The point made (about threefold variation between people) is correct for the range of values; only the label is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The arm–leg difference in methadone concentration in 25 cases is given as a median of 72 µmol/L (interquartile range 20–200 µmol/L), while the series' concentrations are given as 84–2700 µg/L. At methadone's molar mass of about 309 g/mol, 72 µmol/L is about 22 mg/L, about eight times the highest concentration in the series (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Extrapolation from post-mortem concentrations to ante-mortem concentrations
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit is probably µg/L; the size of the arm–leg difference should be taken from Milroy and Forrest (2000), not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 68, cited for post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios of MDMA (1.1 to 6.6) and MDA (1.5 to 13.3), is Elliott and Burgess (2005) on urine analysis in suspected drink spiking, whose title does not suggest such data. Reference 75, a study of morphine concentrations by collection site in heroin overdose victims, is cited among animal experiments on morphine (the porcine study is reference 78), and reference 82, on the redistribution of selected psychiatric drugs in post-mortem cases, is cited for animal experiments showing little redistribution of moclobemide. References 6 and 83 are the same paper listed twice.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; References 6, 68, 75, 78, 82 and 83
reporting_issues.consequence: The MDMA and MDA ratios cannot be traced to their source from this review, and part of the animal evidence it cites for morphine and moclobemide is cited to papers whose titles describe human deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes its search as systematic and the problems as systematically reviewed, but it reports no selection criteria, numbers of records or synthesis method.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is a narrative review with a documented search and must not be appraised or cited as a systematic review.

reporting_issues.issue: Rouzioux's series is given two ways: 8 of 10 cases with post-mortem left-ventricular concentrations 2.58 to 17.66 times those in life (Site-related and time-related differences, 1st paragraph), and later post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios for four imipramine cases (4.85, 1.39, 9.94 and 7.60) and two chloroquine cases (17.66 and 14.6), one of which (1.39) lies below that minimum.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Site-related and time-related differences in post-mortem concentrations, 1st paragraph; Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sampling site or timing behind the two sets of figures may differ but is not stated; neither range should be cited from this review without Rouzioux (1980, reference 44).
